nodes.statement: We have the following relations of norms for any $\Phi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{F}^d)$. \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] $\Norm[\Phi]_{\infty} \leq q^{\frac{d\delta(\Phi)}{l}} \Norm[\Phi]_l$ and $\Norm[\Phi]_l \leq q^{-\frac{dD(\Phi)}{l}} \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}$. \item[(2)] $\mathcal{S}_l^{\vec{\sigma}}(\Phi) \leq q^{-\norm[\vec{\sigma}] D(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_l$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Sup and ${\rm L}^l$ norms and weighted semi-norms of $\Phi$ are comparable with constants given by $q^{\delta(\Phi)}$ and $q^{-D(\Phi)}$.
conclusions: $\Norm[\Phi]_{\infty} \leq q^{\frac{d\delta(\Phi)}{l}} \Norm[\Phi]_l$ and $\Norm[\Phi]_l \leq q^{-\frac{dD(\Phi)}{l}} \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}$.
$\mathcal{S}_l^{\vec{\sigma}}(\Phi) \leq q^{-\norm[\vec{\sigma}] D(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_l$.
nodes.label: SchEquiv

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.19
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $d=1$; average over $x_0+\mathfrak{p}^{\delta}$ for the first inequality, bound by the support volume for the second, and by the sup of $|x|^\sigma$ on $\mathfrak{p}^D$ for the last.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the case $d=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $d=1$.

nodes.name: First inequality
nodes.statement: Let $x_0 \in \mathbf{F}$ be such that $\norm[\Phi(x_0)] = \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}$, then $$ \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l = {\rm Vol}(\mathfrak{p}^{\delta(\Phi)})^{-1} \int_{x_0 + \mathfrak{p}^{\delta(\Phi)}} \norm[\Phi(x)]^l dx \leq q^{\delta(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_l^l $$ and we get the first inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Average over $x_0+\mathfrak{p}^\delta$.

nodes.name: Second inequality
nodes.statement: The second follows from $$ \Norm[\Phi]_l^l \leq \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l \int_{{\rm supp}(\Phi)} dx \leq \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l \cdot {\rm Vol}(\mathfrak{p}^{D(\Phi)}) = q^{-D(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l. $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound by the volume of the support.

nodes.name: Last inequality
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|x|^\sigma$ on $\mathfrak{p}^D$.

nodes.name: Space ${\rm B}_c(\mathbb{Z};\varpi)$
nodes.statement: For any $c \in \ag{R}$, we define ${\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ to be the space of functions $f: \varpi^{\ag{Z}} \to \ag{C}$ satisfying \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] $\lim_{n \to -\infty} f(\varpi^n) q^{-n\sigma} = 0$ for any $\sigma > 0$. \item[(2)] $\lim_{n \to +\infty} f(\varpi^n) q^{-n \sigma} = 0$ for any $\sigma > c$. \end{itemize} The subspace ${\rm B}_c^0(\ag{Z};\varpi) \subset {\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ is defined by replacing (1) with \begin{itemize} \item[(1')] $f(\varpi^n)=0$ for $n \ll -1$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Space ${\rm H}_c(\mathbb{C};q)$
nodes.statement: For any $c \in \ag{R}$ we define ${\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q)$ to be the space of meromorphic functions $M: \ag{C} \to \ag{C}$ satisfying \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] $M(s+i\frac{2\pi}{\log q}) = M(s)$ for all $s \in \ag{C}$. \item[(2)] $M(s)$ is holomorphic for $\Re s > c$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Semi-norms $B_l^{\sigma}$
Semi-norms $H_l^{\sigma}$
Topology on ${\rm B}_c(\mathbb{Z};\varpi)$ independent of $l$
nodes.statement: The topology on ${\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ defined by $B_l^*$ does not depend on $l$. More precisely, for any $f \in {\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$ $$ B_l^{\sigma}(f) \ll_{\epsilon,l} B_{\infty}^{\sigma-\epsilon}(f) + B_{\infty}^{\sigma+\epsilon}(f); $$ $$ B_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f) \leq B_l^{\sigma}(f). $$
assumptions: for any $f \in {\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$
conclusions: The topology on ${\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ defined by $B_l^*$ does not depend on $l$.
$$ B_l^{\sigma}(f) \ll_{\epsilon,l} B_{\infty}^{\sigma-\epsilon}(f) + B_{\infty}^{\sigma+\epsilon}(f); $$ $$ B_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f) \leq B_l^{\sigma}(f). $$
nodes.label: BEquiv

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.24
nodes.statement: The first follows from $$ B_l^{\sigma}(f)^l \leq B_{\infty}^{\sigma-\epsilon}(f) \sum_{n \geq 0} q^{-n\epsilon} + B_{\infty}^{\sigma+\epsilon}(f) \sum_{n < 0} q^{n\epsilon}. $$ The second is obvious by positivity.
nodes.statement_short: Split the sum at $n=0$; the reverse inequality by positivity.

nodes.name: Topology on ${\rm H}_c(\mathbb{C};q)$ independent of $l$
nodes.statement: The topology on ${\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q)$ defined by $H_l^*$ does not depend on $l$. More precisely, for any $M \in {\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$ $$ H_l^{\sigma}(M) \leq H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(M); $$ $$ H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(M) \ll_{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma-\epsilon}(M) + H_l^{\sigma+\epsilon}(M). $$
assumptions: for any $M \in {\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$
conclusions: The topology on ${\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q)$ defined by $H_l^*$ does not depend on $l$.
$$ H_l^{\sigma}(M) \leq H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(M); $$ $$ H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(M) \ll_{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma-\epsilon}(M) + H_l^{\sigma+\epsilon}(M). $$
nodes.label: HEquiv

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.25
nodes.statement: The first is obvious. For the second, let $s_0$ be any complex number with $\Re s_0 = \sigma$ and $0 < \Im s_0 < 2\pi / \log q$. Selecting the contour joining $\sigma+\epsilon$, $\sigma+\epsilon + i 2\pi / \log q$, $\sigma - \epsilon + i 2\pi / \log q$ and $\sigma-\epsilon$, we see $$ \log q \cdot M(s_0) = \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{M(\sigma+\epsilon+i\tau)}{\sigma+\epsilon+i\tau - s_0} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} - \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{M(\sigma-\epsilon+i\tau)}{\sigma-\epsilon+i\tau - s_0} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi}. $$ Using H\"older inequality we deduce \begin{align*} \log q \cdot \norm[M(s_0)] &\leq \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma+\epsilon}(M) \cdot \left( \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} \right)^{\frac{l-1}{l}} + \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma-\epsilon}(M) \cdot \left( \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} \right)^{\frac{l-1}{l}} \\ &= \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma+\epsilon}(M) + \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma-\epsilon}(M). \end{align*} We conclude by taking $\sup$ with respect to $\Re s_0 = \sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's formula on a rectangle of height one period, then Hölder.

nodes.name: Cauchy formula
nodes.statement: The first is obvious. For the second, let $s_0$ be any complex number with $\Re s_0 = \sigma$ and $0 < \Im s_0 < 2\pi / \log q$. Selecting the contour joining $\sigma+\epsilon$, $\sigma+\epsilon + i 2\pi / \log q$, $\sigma - \epsilon + i 2\pi / \log q$ and $\sigma-\epsilon$, we see $$ \log q \cdot M(s_0) = \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{M(\sigma+\epsilon+i\tau)}{\sigma+\epsilon+i\tau - s_0} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} - \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{M(\sigma-\epsilon+i\tau)}{\sigma-\epsilon+i\tau - s_0} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi}. $$
nodes.statement_short: First inequality trivial; Cauchy integral formula on a period rectangle for the second.

nodes.name: Hölder
nodes.statement: Using H\"older inequality we deduce \begin{align*} \log q \cdot \norm[M(s_0)] &\leq \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma+\epsilon}(M) \cdot \left( \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} \right)^{\frac{l-1}{l}} + \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma-\epsilon}(M) \cdot \left( \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} \right)^{\frac{l-1}{l}} \\ &= \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma+\epsilon}(M) + \frac{1}{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma-\epsilon}(M). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Hölder bound.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: We conclude by taking $\sup$ with respect to $\Re s_0 = \sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the supremum.

nodes.name: Continuity of $q$-Mellin transform and inversion
nodes.statement: The two maps $$ {\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi) \to {\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q), f \mapsto \Mellin{f}(s) = \sum_{n \in \ag{Z}} f(\varpi^n) q^{-ns}, \text{ for } \Re s > c; $$ $$ {\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q) \to {\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi), M \mapsto f_M(\varpi^n) = \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} M(\sigma+i\tau) q^{n(\sigma + i \tau)} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi}, \forall \sigma > c $$ are continuous with respect to the above topologies defined by semi-norms.
nodes.statement_short: The non-archimedean Mellin transform and its inversion are continuous between ${\rm B}_c(\mathbb{Z};\varpi)$ and ${\rm H}_c(\mathbb{C};q)$.
conclusions: The two maps $$ {\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi) \to {\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q), f \mapsto \Mellin{f}(s) = \sum_{n \in \ag{Z}} f(\varpi^n) q^{-ns}, \text{ for } \Re s > c; $$ $$ {\rm H}_c(\ag{C};q) \to {\rm B}_c(\ag{Z};\varpi), M \mapsto f_M(\varpi^n) = \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} M(\sigma+i\tau) q^{n(\sigma + i \tau)} \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi}, \forall \sigma > c $$ are continuous with respect to the above topologies defined by semi-norms.
nodes.label: BHEquiv

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.26
nodes.statement: The continuity follows from $$ H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(\Mellin{f}) \leq \sum_{n \in \ag{Z}} \norm[f(\varpi^n)] q^{-n\sigma} = B_1^{\sigma}(f); $$ $$ B_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f_M) \leq \sup_{n \in \ag{Z}} \int_0^{\frac{2\pi}{\log q}} \norm[M(\sigma+i\tau) q^{n i \tau}] \frac{\log q d\tau}{2\pi} = H_1^{\sigma}(M). $$
nodes.statement_short: Direct bounds $H_\infty\le B_1$ and $B_\infty\le H_1$.

nodes.name: Angular components $f_{\xi}(\varpi^n)$ (non-archimedean)
nodes.statement: Note that the abstract part of Definition \ref{FourF^1} still makes sense in the current case, i.e., for any function $f: \mathbf{F} \to \ag{C}$ and $\xi \in \widehat{\mathbf{F}^1}$ we can define $$ f_{\xi}(\varpi^n) = \int_{\mathbf{F}^1} f(\varpi^n u) \xi(u) du, n \in \ag{Z}. $$

nodes.name: Angular components of Schwartz functions (non-archimedean)
nodes.statement: For any $f \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{F})$, $f_{\xi} \neq 0$ only for $\xi$ satisfying $\mathfrak{c}(\xi) \leq m(f)$, hence for only finitely many $\xi$. We have $f_{\xi} \in B_0^0(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ and $$ B_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f_{\xi}) \leq \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f), \forall \sigma > 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: Only finitely many $\xi$ (conductor $\le m(f)$) give nonzero $f_\xi$, each in ${\rm B}_0^0$ with $B_\infty^\sigma(f_\xi)\le\mathcal{S}_\infty^\sigma(f)$.
conclusions: $f_{\xi} \neq 0$ only for $\xi$ satisfying $\mathfrak{c}(\xi) \leq m(f)$, hence for only finitely many $\xi$.
We have $f_{\xi} \in B_0^0(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ and $$ B_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f_{\xi}) \leq \mathcal{S}_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f), \forall \sigma > 0. $$

nodes.statement: Obvious.
nodes.statement_short: Stated as obvious.

nodes.name: Non-archimedean bound for the integral $\int\Phi(t,y/t)\ldots$
nodes.statement: For any $\Phi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{F}^2)$, $s \in \ag{C}$, $\sigma > \max(0,-2\Re s)$ and $\epsilon > 0$ with $\sigma-\epsilon, \sigma+2\Re s - \epsilon >0$, there is $N=N(\epsilon, \sigma, \sigma+2\Re s) > 0$ such that with implied constant depending only on $\epsilon$ $$ \extnorm{ \int_{\mathbf{F}^{\times}} \Phi(t,\frac{y}{t}) \omega^{-1}\xi^2(t)\norm[t]_{\mathbf{F}}^{2s} d^{\times}t } \ll_{\epsilon} q^{-ND(\Phi)+m(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty} \cdot \norm[y]_{\mathbf{F}}^{-\sigma} 1_{y \in \mathfrak{p}^{2D(\Phi)}}. $$

nodes.statement:
Writing $D_v=\min(D(\Phi_v), -\mathfrak{c}(\psi_v)-\delta(\Phi_v))$ for $v<\infty$, it follows from Proposition ef{LocWhiBdA} and ef{LocWhiBdNA} that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $N \gg 1$ $$ \extnorm{W_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};na(y)\kappa)} \ll_{\epsilon,N,\Phi} \prod_{v \mid \infty} \min(

nodes.name: Rapid decay of the non-constant part of Eisenstein series
nodes.statement: For any $\Phi \in \mathcal{S}(\ag{A}^2)$, $m \in \ag{N}$ and any $\sigma > \norm[\Re s]$, we have $$ \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} \left( {\rm E}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) - {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) \right)} \leq \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbf{F}^{\times}} \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} W_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};a(\alpha)g)} \ll_{\sigma,\Phi} {\rm Ht}(g)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\sigma}, $$ which is of rapid decay with respect to ${\rm Ht}(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: All $s$-derivatives of ${\rm E}-{\rm E}_N$ are $\ll{\rm Ht}(g)^{-1/2-\sigma}$ for every $\sigma>|\Re s|$, hence of rapid decay.
conclusions: $$ \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} \left( {\rm E}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) - {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) \right)} \leq \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbf{F}^{\times}} \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} W_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};a(\alpha)g)} \ll_{\sigma,\Phi} {\rm Ht}(g)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\sigma}, $$ which is of rapid decay with respect to ${\rm Ht}(g)$.

nodes.name: $K$-isotypic expansion of $f$
nodes.statement: Consider $f \in V_{\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}}^{\infty}$ and take its Fourier expansion into $\gp{K}$-isotypic types $$ f = \sum_{\vec{n}} \hat{f}_{\vec{n}} \cdot e_{\vec{n}}(\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}) $$ for some $\hat{f}_{\vec{n}} \in \ag{C}$, where $e_{\vec{n}}(\xi,\omega\xi^{-1})$ is unitary with $\gp{K}$-type parametrized by $\vec{n}$ as in \cite[Section 3.5]{Wu5}.

nodes.name: Intertwining coefficients $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$
nodes.statement: For $\Re s \gg 1$, we have $$ {\rm E}_{\gp{N}}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f) = f(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}) + \sum_{\vec{n}} \hat{f}_{\vec{n}} \cdot \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}) e_{\vec{n}}(-s,\omega\xi^{-1},\xi), $$ where $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ are the explicit coefficients of the intertwining operator on the $\gp{K}$-type $\vec{n}$ part as in \textit{loc.cit.}
nodes.statement_short: The constant term is $f_s$ plus the intertwined section, whose $K$-type components are scaled by explicit coefficients $\mu(s;\vec n)$.

nodes.name: Poles of the intertwining coefficients
nodes.statement: The possible poles of the collection of meromorphic functions $\{ \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}) : \vec{n} \}$ are \begin{itemize} \item The pole of $\Lambda(1-2s,\omega\xi^{-2})$ at $s=(1+i\mu(\omega\xi^{-2}))/2$ with order at most $1$, when $\omega\xi^{-2}$ is trivial on $\ag{A}^{(1)}$ and $\vec{n}=\vec{0}$. We call this pole the \emph{spherical pole}. \item The (both trivial and non-trivial) zeros of $L(1+2s,\omega^{-1}\xi^2)$ with order at most that of the zero. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Poles of $\mu(s;\vec n)$: the simple spherical pole at $(1+i\mu)/2$ for $\vec n=0$, and zeros of $L(1+2s,\omega^{-1}\xi^2)$.
conclusions: The pole of $\Lambda(1-2s,\omega\xi^{-2})$ at $s=(1+i\mu(\omega\xi^{-2}))/2$ with order at most $1$, when $\omega\xi^{-2}$ is trivial on $\ag{A}^{(1)}$ and $\vec{n}=\vec{0}$. We call this pole the \emph{spherical pole}.
The (both trivial and non-trivial) zeros of $L(1+2s,\omega^{-1}\xi^2)$ with order at most that of the zero.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.31
nodes.statement: This can be seen either from our explicit computation of $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ in \cite{Wu5}, or from (\ref{RelSec}) and $$ \mathcal{M} f_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}) = f_{\widehat{\Phi}}(-s,\omega\xi^{-1},\xi), $$ which is meromorphic with a simple pole at $s=(1+i\mu(\omega\xi^{-2}))/2$ (the other pole is cancelled by that of $f_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1})$) by Tate's theory.
nodes.statement_short: From the explicit computation in [Wu5], or from (5.1) and Tate's theory.

nodes.name: Polynomial bound for intertwining coefficients
nodes.statement: Assume $\mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}_0)$ has a pole at $s_0$ with order $n$ ($n=0$ if it is holomorphic at $s_0$) for some $\vec{n}_0$. Define $$ \Norm[\vec{n}] = \prod_v (\norm[n_v]+1) \text{ for } \vec{n} = (n_v)_v. $$ Then as $s$ lying in any small compact neighborhood $K$ of $s_0$ where no other pole occur, we have $$ \extnorm{(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})} \ll \Norm[\vec{n}]^N $$ for some $N$ and the implied constant depending only on $K$, $\xi$ and $\omega\xi^{-1}$ (i.e., independent of $\vec{n}$).
nodes.statement_short: Near a pole of order $n$, $(s-s_0)^n\mu(s;\vec n)$ grows at most polynomially in $\|\vec n\|$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.33
nodes.statement: The lemma shows that $(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ is polynomially increasing in $\vec{n}$. But $\hat{f}_{\vec{n}}$ is rapidly decreasing in $\vec{n}$ by smoothness of $f$. The sum over $\vec{n}$ is thus absolutely and uniformly convergent for $s$ lying in $K$, hence defines an analytic function in $s$. By uniqueness of analytic continuation, we get the first equation. The rest follows from the polynomial increase of $(s-s_0)^n \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n})$ and Cauchy's integral formula for derivatives.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomial growth of coefficients against rapid decay of $\hat f_{\vec n}$ gives uniform convergence; analytic continuation and Cauchy's formula conclude.

Then $$ f_0(\kappa) = \lim_{s \to s_0} \frac{(s-s_0)\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2(s_0-s)}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2-2(s_0-s)))} \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) d\kappa = - \frac{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}^*(0)}{\Lambda_{\mathbf{F}}(2)} \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) d\kappa. $$

nodes.name: Principal congruence subgroup $\Gamma(N)$
nodes.statement: It is well-known that there is an exact sequence $$ 1 \to \Gamma(N) \to {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z}) \to {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z}/N\ag{Z}) \to 1, $$ where $\Gamma(N)$ is called the principal congruence subgroup of ${\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ modulo $N$.

nodes.name: Subgroups $\Gamma_0(N)$ and $\Gamma_0^-(N)$
nodes.statement: The pre-image of the upper resp. lower triangular subgroup of ${\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z}/N\ag{Z})$ in ${\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ is denoted by $\Gamma_0(N)$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N)$, which includes $\Gamma(N)$ as a normal subgroup.

nodes.name: Unipotent matrices $n_r^{\pm}(\vec\alpha)$
nodes.statement: For $\vec{\alpha} \in \ag{Z}^{r-1}$ realized as a column vector, we define matrices, with $I_k$ denoting the identity matrix of rank $k$ $$ n_r^+(\vec{\alpha}) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{\alpha}^T \\ \vec{0} & I_{r-1} \end{pmatrix}, n_r^-(\vec{\alpha}) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{0}^T \\ \vec{\alpha} & I_{r-1} \end{pmatrix}. $$

nodes.name: Coset representatives for $\Gamma_0(N)$
nodes.statement: Any coset of $\Gamma_0(N) \backslash {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N) \backslash {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ has a representative of the form $N_- N_+$ resp. $N_+N_-$, where $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ is lower resp. upper unipotent with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every coset of $\Gamma_0(N)\backslash{\rm SL}_r(\mathbb{Z})$ has a representative $N_-N_+$ with unipotent factors having entries in $[-N/2,N/2]$.
conclusions: Any coset of $\Gamma_0(N) \backslash {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N) \backslash {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$ has a representative of the form $N_- N_+$ resp. $N_+N_-$, where $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ is lower resp. upper unipotent with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$.
nodes.label: CongGpLemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.35
nodes.statement: We treat the case for $\Gamma_0(N)$. Take any $A \in {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$. Let the first column of $A$ be $(a_1,\cdots,a_r)^T \in \ag{Z}^r$. Then we have ${\rm lcd}(a_1,\cdots,a_r)=1$, which implies the existence of $u_i \in \ag{Z}$ such that $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i a_i = 1$. In particular, we have ${\rm lcd}(u_1,a_2,\cdots,a_r)=1$. For any $k_j \in \ag{Z}, 2 \leq j \leq r$, the substitution $$ u_1' = u_1+\sum_{j=2}^r k_j a_j; u_j' = u_j-k_j, 2 \leq j \leq r $$ still gives $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i' a_i = 1$. By an iterative application of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progression, we can choose $k_j$'s such that $u_1'$ is a prime number as large as we want. In particular, we can make ${\rm lcd}(u_1',N)=1$. Since ${\rm lcd}(u_1',\cdots,u_r')=1$, at least one of $u_j', 2 \leq j \leq r$, say $u_2'$, is coprime with $u_1'$. Hence ${\rm lcd}(u_1',Nu_2')=1$ and we can find $v_1,v_2 \in \ag{Z}$ such that $u_1'v_2-Nu_2'v_1=1$. The matrix $$ B = \begin{pmatrix} u_1' & u_2' & u_3' \cdots \\ Nv_1 & v_2 & 0 \cdots \\ \vec{0} & \vec{0} & I_{r-2} \end{pmatrix} \in \Gamma_0(N) $$ and gives, for some $A'=\tilde{A}-\vec{\alpha} \vec{\beta_1}^T \in {\rm SL}_{r-1}(\ag{Z})$, that $$ BA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{\beta_1}^T \\ \vec{\alpha} & \tilde{A} \end{pmatrix} \Rightarrow A \in \Gamma_0(N) \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \\ \vec{\alpha} & A' \end{pmatrix} n_r^+(\vec{\beta_1}). $$ Repeating the process on $A'$ or making an induction on $r$ we then find successively $\vec{\beta_k} \in \ag{Z}^{r-k}$ such that for some lower unipotent $N_-^1$ $$ A \in \Gamma_0(N) N_-^1 N_+^1, N_+^1=\prod_{k=0}^{r-2} \begin{pmatrix} I_k & 0 \\ 0 & n_{r-k}^+(\vec{\beta_{k+1}}) \end{pmatrix}. $$ Taking $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$ such that $N_-^1 \equiv N_- \pmod{N}$ resp. $N_+^1 \equiv N_+ \pmod{N}$, we then find $N_-^1 N_-^{-1}, N_+^1 N_+^{-1} \in \Gamma(N)$ and conclude by its normality.
nodes.statement_short: Use Dirichlet's theorem to build $B\in\Gamma_0(N)$ clearing the first column of $A$, iterate by induction on $r$, then reduce the unipotent factors mod $N$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We treat the case for $\Gamma_0(N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Treat $\Gamma_0(N)$ only.

nodes.name: Bezout coefficients
nodes.statement: Take any $A \in {\rm SL}_r(\ag{Z})$. Let the first column of $A$ be $(a_1,\cdots,a_r)^T \in \ag{Z}^r$. Then we have ${\rm lcd}(a_1,\cdots,a_r)=1$, which implies the existence of $u_i \in \ag{Z}$ such that $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i a_i = 1$. In particular, we have ${\rm lcd}(u_1,a_2,\cdots,a_r)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $A$ and Bezout coefficients $u_i$ for its first column.

nodes.name: Substitution
nodes.statement: For any $k_j \in \ag{Z}, 2 \leq j \leq r$, the substitution $$ u_1' = u_1+\sum_{j=2}^r k_j a_j; u_j' = u_j-k_j, 2 \leq j \leq r $$ still gives $\Sigma_{i=1}^r u_i' a_i = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Modify the coefficients by a substitution preserving the relation.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's theorem
nodes.statement: By an iterative application of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progression, we can choose $k_j$'s such that $u_1'$ is a prime number as large as we want. In particular, we can make ${\rm lcd}(u_1',N)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet's theorem makes $u_1'$ a large prime coprime to $N$.

nodes.name: Find $v_1,v_2$
nodes.statement: Since ${\rm lcd}(u_1',\cdots,u_r')=1$, at least one of $u_j', 2 \leq j \leq r$, say $u_2'$, is coprime with $u_1'$. Hence ${\rm lcd}(u_1',Nu_2')=1$ and we can find $v_1,v_2 \in \ag{Z}$ such that $u_1'v_2-Nu_2'v_1=1$.

nodes.name: Matrix $B$
nodes.statement: The matrix $$ B = \begin{pmatrix} u_1' & u_2' & u_3' \cdots \\ Nv_1 & v_2 & 0 \cdots \\ \vec{0} & \vec{0} & I_{r-2} \end{pmatrix} \in \Gamma_0(N) $$ and gives, for some $A'=\tilde{A}-\vec{\alpha} \vec{\beta_1}^T \in {\rm SL}_{r-1}(\ag{Z})$, that $$ BA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{\beta_1}^T \\ \vec{\alpha} & \tilde{A} \end{pmatrix} \Rightarrow A \in \Gamma_0(N) \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \\ \vec{\alpha} & A' \end{pmatrix} n_r^+(\vec{\beta_1}). $$
nodes.statement_short: Build $B\in\Gamma_0(N)$ reducing $A$ to block form.

nodes.name: Induction on $r$
nodes.statement: Repeating the process on $A'$ or making an induction on $r$ we then find successively $\vec{\beta_k} \in \ag{Z}^{r-k}$ such that for some lower unipotent $N_-^1$ $$ A \in \Gamma_0(N) N_-^1 N_+^1, N_+^1=\prod_{k=0}^{r-2} \begin{pmatrix} I_k & 0 \\ 0 & n_{r-k}^+(\vec{\beta_{k+1}}) \end{pmatrix}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $r$ gives $A\in\Gamma_0(N)N_-^1N_+^1$.

nodes.name: Reduce mod $N$
nodes.statement: Taking $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$ such that $N_-^1 \equiv N_- \pmod{N}$ resp. $N_+^1 \equiv N_+ \pmod{N}$, we then find $N_-^1 N_-^{-1}, N_+^1 N_+^{-1} \in \Gamma(N)$ and conclude by its normality.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce entries mod $N$ using normality of $\Gamma(N)$.

nodes.name: Degree $r=r_1+2r_2$
nodes.statement: Let $[\mathbf{F}:\ag{Q}]=r=r_1+2r_2$ where $r_1$ resp. $2r_2$ is the number of embeddings of $\mathbf{F}$ into real resp. complex numbers.

nodes.name: Canonical embedding $\sigma: \mathbf{F}\to\mathbb{R}^r$
nodes.statement: Recall that we have a canonical map by choosing one complex embedding $\sigma_{r_1+j}, 1 \leq j \leq r_2$ in a pair conjugate to each other by complex conjugation $$ \sigma: \mathbf{F} \to \ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2} \simeq \ag{R}^r, $$ $$ \sigma(x) = (\sigma_1(x), \cdots, \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x)) = (\sigma_1(x), \cdots, \sigma_{r_1}(x), \Re \sigma_{r_1+1}(x), \Im \sigma_{r_1+1}(x), \cdots, \Re \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x), \Im \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x)). $$

nodes.name: Function $f_c$
nodes.statement: For $c \gg 1$, we define a functions $f_c$ on $\ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2}$ by $$ f_c(\vec{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^{r_1} \min(1, \norm[x_i]^{-c}) \prod_{j=1}^{r_2} \min(1, \norm[x_{r_1+j}]^{-2c}), \vec{x}=(x_i)_{1\leq i \leq r_1+r_2}. $$

nodes.name: Lattice sum estimates for $f_c$
nodes.statement_short: Two bounds for $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathfrak{J}^{-1}}f_c(t\sigma(\alpha))$, polynomial in the norm of $\mathfrak{J}$.
conclusions: $ \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1} - \{0\}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) \ll_{\mathbf{F},c} \norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^{3c} t^{-c} $
$ \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) \ll_{\mathbf{F},c} t^{-r} \norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^{-1} \left( 1+t\frac{\norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^2}{\sqrt{r}} \right)^{rc} $
nodes.label: GTechEstClassical

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.36
nodes.statement_short: (1) Compare $f_c$ with norms, control the lattice basis by elementary divisors and Lemma 5.35, sum $\|\vec n\|^{-c}$; (2) compare the sum with an integral using the fundamental parallelogram's diameter.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement_short: Part (1): norm comparison, basis control via Lemma 5.35, then lattice sum.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: (2) If $\mathcal{L}$ is a lattice in $\ag{R}^r$ with a basis given by the column vectors in a matrix $A_{\mathcal{L}} \in {\rm GL}_r(\ag{R})$, we define its diameter $d(\mathcal{L})$ associated to this basis as the diameter of the fundamental parallelogram spanned by this basis, i.e., $$ d(\mathcal{L}) = \max_{-1 \leq \lambda_i \leq 1, 1\leq i \leq r} \Norm[A_{\mathcal{L}} \vec{\lambda}]_2. $$ Thus we have obviously $d(\mathcal{L}) \leq \sqrt{r} \Norm[A_{\mathcal{L}}]_2$. The same argument in the last part of (1) gives, for some choice of basis of $\mathfrak{J}^{-1}$, that $$ d(\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})) \leq \sqrt{r} \Norm[A_{\mathfrak{o}}]_2 \norm[d_1]^{-1} \left( r+\frac{r(r-1)d_r^2}{8d_1^2} \right). $$ It is also easy to see that for $\vec{x},\vec{y}$ in the same translate of a parallelogram $\vec{x_0}+\mathcal{P}$ of $t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})$, we have $$ \frac{f_c(\vec{x})}{f_c(\vec{y})} \leq 2^{2r_2c} \left( \frac{r_1+r_2+\sqrt{r}d(t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1}))}{r} \right)^{rc}. $$ We thus conclude by \begin{align*} {\rm Vol}(\ag{R}^r/t\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1})) \sum_{\alpha \in \mathfrak{J}^{-1}} f_c(t\sigma(\alpha)) &\leq 2^{2r_2c} \left( \frac{r_1+r_2+t\sqrt{r}d(\sigma(\mathfrak{J}^{-1}))}{r} \right)^{rc} \int_{\ag{R}^r} f_c(\vec{x}) d\vec{x} \\ &\ll_{\mathbf{F},c} \left( 1+t\frac{\norm[\mathfrak{o}/\mathfrak{J}]^2}{\sqrt{r}} \right)^{rc}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Part (2): compare the lattice sum with an integral.

nodes.name: Valuation $v(\mathfrak{J})$
nodes.statement: We shall write, denoting by $\mathfrak{p}_v$ the prime ideal corresponding to $v<\infty$, $v(\mathfrak{J}) \in \ag{N}$ such that $$ \mathfrak{J} = \prod_{v<\infty} \mathfrak{p}_v^{v(\mathfrak{J})}. $$

nodes.name: Adelic lattice sum estimate
nodes.statement_short: Adelic version of Lemma 5.36: the sum over $\alpha\in\mathbf{F}^\times$ of products of local truncated powers is bounded in terms of $|y|_{\mathbb A}$ and the norm of $\mathfrak{J}$.
nodes.label: GTechEst

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.37
nodes.statement_short: Split $|\cdot|_{\mathbb A}$ by a section, reduce via class group representatives and Dirichlet's unit theorem to a lattice sum of $f_{c_2-c_1}$, then apply Lemma 5.36.

nodes.name: Section
nodes.statement: The following exact sequence is split with a splitting section $s: \ag{R}_+ \to \ag{A}^{\times}$ $$ 1 \to \ag{A}^{(1)} \to \ag{A}^{\times} \xrightarrow{|\cdot|_{\ag{A}}} \ag{R}_+ \to 1 $$ such that the image of $s$ is contained in $\ag{A}_{\infty}^{\times} = \prod_{v \mid \infty} \mathbf{F}_v^{\times}$. For any $t \in \ag{R}_+$, we write $t^+=s(t)$ with $t_v^+=t^{1/r} \in \ag{R}_+ \subset \mathbf{F}_v$, such that $$ |t^+|_{\ag{A}} = \prod_{v \mid \infty} |t_v^+|_v = t. $$
nodes.statement_short: Split the idelic norm by an archimedean section $t\mapsto t^+$.

nodes.name: Class group reduction
nodes.statement_short: Write $y$ via class group representatives $\tau$, $\delta_\tau$, $\beta$.

By Dirichlet's unit theorem, we can adjust $u \in \mathfrak{o}^{	imes}$ so that each $
orm[u^{-1} eta_0^{-1}y_v' ]_v$ remains in a compact set in $\ag{R}_+$ depending only on $\mathbf{F}$. orm[\alpha t_v^+]_v^{-(c_2-c_1)} \cdot
